title: MA9-07487
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant XXXXX XXXXX is a citizen of Mexico. He is claiming refugee protection under section 96 and paragraph 97(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
The claimant stated the following during his testimony:
On XXXXX XXXXX, 2009, he allegedly left the XXXXX region, in the state of XXXXX, and he and his friend XXXXX travelled to the state of XXXXX in his truck.

On that trip, the claimant was carrying his briefcase containing his passport and identification papers and many important documents-property title certificates for his eight or so parcels of land, as well as invoices for his trucks and tractors. His friend, who was working at the XXXXX XXXXX, was carrying a quantity of work-related documents and information.
While passing through the XXXXX region, the claimant and his friend were allegedly chased by another truck and forced to stop. The claimant's truck was also allegedly shot at repeatedly.

The claimant and his friend were then allegedly held, searched and robbed by armed men who then took all their personal possessions, including the claimant's briefcase. They then apparently ordered the claimant and his friend to start running, and then they fired at them.

The claimant and his friend apparently managed to escape safe and sound. After wandering for a while, they allegedly managed to find the claimant's truck, which had been left in the same place by the criminals-it is the only thing that the criminals did not take, as they could not [translation] "find" the truck's ignition key, which was in the claimant's pant pocket. The claimant and his friend then allegedly headed for XXXXX in XXXXX. They apparently hid at a gas station and, on three occasions, saw the truck of the criminals who attacked them [translation] "drive by."

While at the gas station, the claimant and his friend supposedly told the people there about their problems. That is when their suspicions were apparently confirmed: their attackers were members of Los Zetas.

The claimant and his friend then allegedly left the area and went to stay with the claimant's parents in XXXXX. They arrived early in the morning of XXXXX, 2009. Then, with the claimant's brother XXXXX, they allegedly went to file a complaint with the public ministry. The judge who took their deposition supposedly told them, then and there, not to recount the facts as they had occurred, because Los Zetas had informants in the area. He allegedly suggested that they should claim to have been robbed while in the washroom at the gas station.

The claimant and his friend then apparently agreed to provide a false version of the facts for their complaint. However, in the complaint they both allegedly mentioned the belongings that were stolen from them during that incident.

The claimant and his friend then allegedly left XXXXX and went to hide at the claimant's stepfather's home in XXXXX. When they arrived, he apparently told them [translation] "that someone came at dawn to get me."1
The claimant stated that he hid in several different locations over the next few weeks. He also allegedly learned during this time that someone was looking for him.

On XXXXX, 2009, while the claimant was back in the XXXXX region, he was allegedly abducted by two members of Los Zetas, who stole US$ XXXXX from him. However, the claimant states in his Personal Information Form (PIF) that it was XXXXX pesos.2 The claimant was also allegedly threatened that it was going to [translation] "cost you more for trying to mock us." They also allegedly told him to sell his tractor because [translation] "they were going to pass off the money."3
After he was released, the claimant allegedly decided to leave Mexico. He arrived in Canada on XXXXX, 2009, and claimed refugee protection upon his arrival.
The claimant fears extortion and vengeance from Los Zetas if he were to return to his country, because they are allegedly still looking for him in his country. Ultimately, he fears death.
The claimant's claim for refugee protection is rejected because the risk that he alleges is a generalized risk. ANALYSIS Identity
The panel is satisfied as to the claimant's identity since a copy of his Mexican passport was submitted on file under A-2, in a bundle. Inapplicability of section 96 of the IRPA

Section 96 of the IRPA does not apply in this case. The claimant's fear stems from criminality. He is not targeted on one of the five Convention grounds since he alleged a fear of extortion and vengeance by Los Zetas, an organization involved primarily in organized crime.
Since the state is in no way involved in the actual harm feared by the claimant, paragraph 97(1)(a) of the IRPA, namely the danger of torture, also does not apply.

The following analysis will therefore look at whether or not there is a risk under paragraph 97(1)(b) of the IRPA, that is, whether there is a risk to his life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, should the claimant return to his country today. Paragraph 97(1)(b) of the IRPA Claimant's testimony

The panel asked the claimant a number of questions in order to understand why-two and a half years after first being confronted by the members of Los Zetas on XXXXX, 2009-he still fears returning to Mexico.

The panel especially dwelled on the currency of the fear, given that that his friend XXXXX -who was also allegedly present and was threatened and robbed along with the claimant during the attack of XXXXX 2009-has been living in Mexico since this incident and has not had any particular problems. Although Los Zetas had his documents and personal contact information, they never harassed him again.

The claimant was quite assertive: because they have his personal information and contact information [translation] "Los Zetas can easily find me." And they are [translation] "interested only in money." Consequently, XXXXX, who is just [translation] "an employee," is not "of interest to Los Zetas." However, [translation] "I have a lot of possessions."

The claimant went on to explain that Los Zetas would have been aware of this fact since they would have found many [translation] "property title certificates in my name and invoices for trucks and tractors" that belonged to him in the briefcase that they stole from him. To conclude, the claimant stated that [translation] "they also stole $ XXXXX from me." Consequently, should he return to Mexico today, these Los Zetas members would continue to harass him in order to extort more money from him. Furthermore, they could kill him should he fail to comply.

During his testimony, the claimant also stated that Los Zetas also want [translation] "vengeance" against him-to the point of wanting to kill him-because he dared to retrieve his truck after the attack on XXXXX, 2009, whereas, according to their internal rules, that truck had become theirs. Current situation in Mexico (generalized risk)

After analyzing the facts in this case, the panel is of the opinion that, even if the claimant is subjected to a risk to his life should he return to his country today, this is a generalized risk within the meaning of subparagraph 97(1)(b)(ii).

No evidence, regardless of how minimal, could lead the panel to believe that the risk that the claimant might face would be different from the risk currently faced by the entire population of his country, which is faced with serious criminality throughout its territory.4

The evidence5 demonstrates that people from all levels of Mexican society are currently at risk of being victims of serious criminality, which is rampant in Mexico. This is largely due to corruption and the presence of drug cartels and many criminal gangs.
Los Zetas is one of many criminal organizations active in Mexico.6

The presence of organized crime in Mexico has meant that robbery, abduction, extortion and other criminal activities have become commonplace. These violent acts all result from the generalized criminality that exists in Mexico.

In this case, the panel is of the opinion that the claimant was a victim of Los Zetas in XXXXX 2009. The panel also notes that, even if this attack initially appeared to be random, the subsequent incident, namely the claimant's detainment in XXXXX 2009, targeted him personally. Los Zetas knew that he had money. They then robbed him of $ XXXXX and threatened him with extortion.
Seen in this light, it is logical to believe that, should the claimant return to his country, he could once again be personally targeted, since he would represent a source of revenue for Los Zetas.

However, even if the claimant was personally targeted in the past (robbery, detainment and extortion attempts); even if he filed a complaint with the public ministry; and even if, upon his return to his country, he could be personally targeted because of his [translation] "privileged" financial situation (either because of the land that he owns or because of his other property), this is insufficient to warrant granting him the status of a person in need of protection under paragraph 97(1)(b) of the IRPA, since all the threats that he faces are the result of violent acts committed in Mexico in a context of generalized criminality.7

As such, the panel cannot ignore the existing case law establishing that a victim of crime who is targeted specifically or even known and identified personally by criminals because the victim has apparently been a profitable source of income for them in the past cannot be said to face a different risk within the meaning of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, since the risk remains essentially a generalized risk based on criminality that is present throughout an area..8

Even if the claimant is part of a demographic subgroup, that of people with financial means or landowners, the risk of extortion with which he was and could be confronted, should he return to his country, remains a generalized risk that all inhabitants of Mexico face on a daily basis.9

One final point: the vengeance that the claimant fears from Los Zetas, because he allegedly [translation] "had the nerve" to take his truck back after the attack of XXXXX 2009, cannot be qualified as a risk that is different from that which the Mexican population as a whole faces.

Even if the particular reason that the claimant might risk being confronted by Los Zetas is different from other Mexican inhabitants' particular reasons, insofar as the nature of the risk is the same (namely the violence, which can go so far as to include murder) and the basis of this risk is the same (namely the failure to comply with Los Zetas' demands), the risk remains a generalized risk. He is therefore a person described in the exception in subparagraph 97(1)(b)(ii) of the IRPA.10 CONCLUSION

For all of these reasons, the claim for refugee protection is rejected.
